oil.summary: Crude sold off sharply on Tuesday, with Brent shedding 5.37% to $87.22 and WTI dropping 3.20% to $82.29, as Pakistani-mediated diplomacy rekindled hopes of a US-Iran negotiation breakthrough and pushed Brent back from an earlier spike near $93.77. RBOB gasoline was the standout mover, cratering 10.65% on the day and over 12% on the month, signalling demand-side concern. Despite persistent Hormuz tension — Iran threatening 45 tankers with fines and confiscation, and a tanker strike reported off Oman — markets chose to price in de-escalation risk rather than supply disruption. On the supply side, Ukraine confirmed a fresh drone strike on Russia's Afipsky refinery in Krasnodar, and Rystad Energy cut its 2026 Russian crude output forecast to 8.95 million bpd. India's import bill continues to surge on quadrupled freight rates, while Sinopec flagged crumbling domestic fuel demand driven by China's EV boom. CME options markets price a 77% chance of an OPEC cut at the next meeting.
drivers: Iran negotiation hopes (Pakistani mediation) triggered a sharp risk-off reversal in crude despite ongoing Hormuz tanker threats
Ukraine drone strikes on Russian refineries tighten global refined-product supply; Rystad cuts Russia 2026 output forecast to 8.95 mb/d
Demand headwinds building: Sinopec flags collapsing Chinese fuel sales amid EV growth; RBOB gasoline -10.65% on the day

gas.summary: Henry Hub edged up 2.37% to $2.849/MMBtu, extending a modest but consistent monthly grind higher of nearly 3%. TTF pulled back 3.21% to €66.125/MWh on the day, though it remains up 13.51% over the past month, reflecting lingering European supply anxiety. The Hormuz crisis is reshaping long-term LNG investment calculus: Equinor cited the Middle East conflict as a factor making its $42 billion Tanzania LNG project more commercially attractive. On the supply side, Norway started production from the second stage of Troll Phase 3, accelerating 55 billion cubic metres from the Troll West reservoir — described as buying Europe time rather than adding new supply. The BLM scheduled an October lease sale covering 3,388 acres in Montana and the Dakotas. News flow for this sector is relatively thin today.
drivers: TTF daily pullback of 3.21% despite a strong monthly uptrend (+13.51%), reflecting short-term profit-taking amid Hormuz de-escalation signals
Hormuz disruption elevating long-term LNG project appeal: Equinor flags Tanzania's $42 bn project as increasingly attractive
Norway's Troll Phase 3 Stage 2 online, accelerating 55 bcm — supportive for European supply but not incremental new volume

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs gained 1.96% to $80.04, building on a 3.40% weekly advance, as TTF's monthly surge of 13.51% keeps gas-to-power switching economics in focus and supports marginal carbon pricing. The day's most structurally significant headline was the reported acceleration of next-generation nuclear development in the US, with Big Tech and private equity channelling capital into advanced nuclear to meet AI data-centre power demand. On the periphery, Ukraine's ongoing drone campaign against Russian refineries and the Hormuz standoff continue to apply upward pressure on fossil-fuel input costs for power generators. The BLM's October lease sale in Montana and the Dakotas is a modest incremental signal for domestic gas-fired generation supply. Overall, the power and carbon data flow today is limited beyond the nuclear-AI theme and the carbon price move.
drivers: EUA carbon up 1.96% on the day and +3.40% on the week, supported by elevated TTF gas costs lifting marginal power-sector abatement costs
AI-driven nuclear revival: Big Tech and private equity accelerating US next-gen nuclear investment to meet surging data-centre electricity demand
Hormuz and Ukraine refinery disruptions sustain elevated fossil-fuel input cost risk for power generators globally
